summary: The note covers deficiency of L-gulonolactone oxidase (GULO), the enzyme that makes the precursor to vitamin C. Its gene was lost independently in haplorhine primates (including humans), guinea pigs, and some bats, leaving a pseudogene (GULOP). It also discusses possible adaptations after the loss, animal and plant models, and related sugar-1,4-lactone oxidases.
one_line: GULO, the enzyme for vitamin C synthesis, was lost independently in humans and other haplorhine primates, guinea pigs and some bats, with evolutionary consequences and research models.
key_facts: The non-functional gulonolactone oxidase pseudogene (GULOP) was mapped to human chromosome 8p21.
GULO produces the precursor to ascorbic acid, which spontaneously converts to the vitamin itself.
GULO activity has been lost independently in several species, including some bats, guinea pigs, and the haplorrhine primates.
Loss of GULO activity in primates occurred about 63 million years ago, around the split into suborders Haplorhini (lost the enzyme) and Strepsirrhini (retained it).
Haplorhines include tarsiers and simians; strepsirrhines include lorises, galagos, pottos, and to some extent lemurs.
OMIM describes L-gulonolactone oxidase deficiency, called 'hypoascorbemia', as 'a public inborn error of metabolism' affecting all humans; its pathological form is scurvy.
Guinea pigs lost the ability to make GULO 20 million years ago.
Linus Pauling observed that apo(a) and Lp(a) were greatly favored by evolution after loss of endogenous ascorbate production, acting as ascorbate surrogate.

Johnson et al. hypothesized that GULOP mutation benefited early primates by increasing uric acid levels and enhancing fructose effects on weight gain and fat accumulation, giving a survival advantage when food was short.
In 1999, Maeda et al. genetically engineered mice with inactivated GULO gene; they depend entirely on dietary vitamin C and show compromised vasculature integrity.
Only primates share regulation of CAMP gene expression by vitamin D, which occurred after the loss of the GULO gene.
Overexpressing inositol oxygenase and gulono-1,4-lactone oxidase in Arabidopsis thaliana leads to enhanced biomass and tolerance to abiotic stresses.
GULO belongs to a family of sugar-1,4-lactone oxidases that includes yeast D-arabinono-1,4-lactone oxidase (ALO), which produces erythorbic acid.
